title: Core Capstone: Putting It All Together (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain the five pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework and name the trade-off behind a design decision.
- Describe the seven methodologies of the Cloud Adoption Framework and what an Azure landing zone is.
- Assemble Nusantara Retail's target architecture from the services of the core month and justify every part.
- Answer "how long can't we sell?" with an RTO and an RPO for each failure scenario.
- Plan your AZ-900 preparation and choose what to study in the deep-dive month.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Four weeks ago you stood in the room next to the pantry, listened to one tired server hum, and heard Ibu Sari's question for the first time: "If that server dies, how long can't we sell?" Nobody in the meeting had an answer.

Since then you have collected the pieces one lunch at a time: regions and availability zones, networks and load balancers, a database that backs itself up, secrets that never touch a configuration file, alerts, policies, budgets, and a Bicep file that can rebuild all of it. What you do not have yet is the whole picture.

The monthly meeting is on Friday. Ibu Sari wants a straight answer with numbers. Dewi wants to know which worries she can hand over to Azure. Pak Budi wants to know how the design sits next to head office, and finance wants a promise that the bill will not surprise anyone. Today you assemble one design, test it against the questions Microsoft's own architects ask, and prepare your answer: how long can't we sell — and how much could we lose?

Reading

A capstone brings no brand-new services. It is the moment the pieces click into place. You will look at Nusantara Retail through two Microsoft frameworks — one for judging a single workload, one for adopting the cloud as a company — then assemble the target architecture, turn it into an answer for the director, and plan your next steps.

1. The Well-Architected Framework: five questions for every design

The Azure Well-Architected Framework (WAF) is Microsoft's collection of design principles, checklists and review tools for building a good workload: the resources, code and data that together deliver one business outcome, such as Nusantara Retail's storefront. The framework groups its guidance into five pillars. The easiest way to remember them is as five questions a demanding reviewer would ask about any design.

Pillar | The reviewer's question | In Nusantara Retail's design | Lunches
Reliability | Does the shop keep selling when something breaks, and can we recover within agreed targets? | Two web VMs in two availability zones behind a Standard load balancer; automatic database backups; a tested failover | 03, 09, 17
Security | Can only the right people and code reach the data? | No public IPs on the VMs; an NSG that admits HTTP only; Microsoft Entra-only database sign-in; Key Vault with Azure RBAC; least privilege for Rizky | 05, 08, 15
Cost Optimization | Are we paying only for what creates value? | Small burstable VMs; a serverless database that pauses; a budget with alerts; tags for cost reports | 01, 19
Operational Excellence | Can we deploy, change, observe and fix it safely and repeatably? | Everything in Bicep, previewed with what-if; alerts that reach a person; a written runbook | 16, 18, 20
Performance Efficiency | Does it keep up when demand changes — during the 12.12 sale, for example? | Scale out by adding servers across zones; right-sized VMs; load tests before peaks | 06, 09, 23

Notice that the pillars are not services. Azure Monitor does not "do" operational excellence, and Key Vault does not "do" security. A pillar is a quality of the whole design, and almost every service you met this month serves more than one. The load balancer, for example, gives you reliability (its health probe routes around failures) and performance efficiency (more servers behind one address) at the same time.

Microsoft publishes the framework as free guidance on Microsoft Learn, including service guides that apply the five pillars to individual services and a self-assessment called the Azure Well-Architected Review. You do not need to read all of it. Ask the five questions of every design you review, starting with your lab today.

Tip: Write down every significant design choice in a few lines: what you chose, which pillar it helps, which pillar it costs, and when to revisit it. Teams call this an architecture decision record. Six months from now nobody will remember why the database pauses itself; the record will.

2. Trade-offs: you cannot max out every pillar

The pillars pull against each other. More redundancy improves reliability and costs money. Private networking improves security and adds moving parts to operate. Auto-pause saves money and makes the first shopper after a quiet hour wait. A good architect does not avoid trade-offs; she chooses them on purpose and explains them to the people who carry the risk.

Decision | Strengthens | Weakens | Nusantara Retail's call
A second web VM in another zone | Reliability | Cost (compute doubles) | Yes. An hour without sales costs more than a month of a small VM.
Zone-redundant database | Reliability | Cost | Yes in production; skipped in the lab.
Serverless database that auto-pauses | Cost | Performance (the first request after a pause waits) | Lab and test only; production keeps a minimum capacity.
Private endpoints instead of public endpoints | Security | Operational excellence (DNS and networking to manage) | Planned for the deep-dive month.
Allowed-locations policy | Security and compliance (data residency) | Agility | Yes — but it must also allow the disaster recovery region.
Long log retention | Operational excellence, security investigations | Cost | 30 days to start; longer for audit logs if regulators ask.

Every "yes" in that table has a price, and every "no" has a risk. Your job is to make both visible. Ibu Sari owns the cost of an outage and finance owns the budget, so they — not you — decide where the line sits, once you have shown them the options in plain words.

Trade-offs also hide in dependencies. A shopper's order needs the public IP, the load balancer, at least one web VM, the database and Key Vault, all at the same moment. If each of those five links were available 99.9% of the time — an illustrative number, not an Azure SLA — the chain as a whole would be available only about 99.5% of the time, because the small gaps add up. That is why the design spends its money where a single failure would stop everything: two VMs instead of one, a zone-redundant front door, a database that survives a zone. Every new dependency, however useful, lowers the total unless it is redundant too.

3. The Cloud Adoption Framework at a glance

The Well-Architected Framework judges one workload. Its companion, the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF), guides the whole organization: the decisions that leaders, platform teams and security teams make before, during and after workloads move to Azure. At the time of writing, CAF describes Azure adoption as seven methodologies, each answering one key question.

Methodology | The key question | Nusantara Retail's answer so far
Strategy | Why are we adopting Azure, and what does success look like? | Stop losing sales to one server, survive the 12.12 peak, keep customer data in Indonesia.
Plan | How will we prepare people and workloads? | Inventory the storefront, the orders database and the store systems; train the team (this course).
Ready | How will we build our Azure landing zone? | Subscriptions, address ranges that avoid head office's 10.0.0.0/16, baseline policies and budgets.
Adopt | How will we migrate, modernize and build workloads? | Move the storefront to VMs now; modernize it to App Service or containers later.
Govern | How will we control the environment? | Allowed locations, required tags, budgets.
Secure | How will we protect it? | Microsoft Entra ID with MFA, Key Vault, Microsoft Defender for Cloud.
Manage | How will we operate and optimize it over time? | Azure Monitor, backups, patching, monthly cost reviews.

The result of the Ready methodology is an Azure landing zone: a prepared, governed environment that workloads move into. Think of a housing estate where the roads, water, electricity and building rules exist before the first house goes up. CAF splits a landing zone in two. The platform landing zone is the shared foundation — the management group hierarchy, identity, connectivity, central monitoring and the policies everyone inherits — usually run by a small platform team. Each workload gets a workload landing zone: the subscriptions where a team like Dewi's builds and runs its application inside the platform's guardrails.

Microsoft offers landing zone accelerators that deploy its recommended designs as code. A company the size of Nusantara Retail can start smaller than the full reference, but it should still decide its management groups, subscriptions, address ranges and baseline policies before the second workload arrives; Lunch 31 builds this out. One reminder from Lunch 18 applies here too: Azure Blueprints is being retired, so today's landing zones are built with infrastructure as code, Azure Policy and deployment stacks.

4. Nusantara Retail's target architecture

Here is the design the core month has been building toward. Production would run in Indonesia Central for data residency; your lab builds the same shape in Southeast Asia.

Walk through it from the outside in:

- The front door. Shoppers reach a zone-redundant Standard public IP on a Standard load balancer (the Basic SKUs were retired in September 2025). An HTTP health probe on /health decides which servers receive new connections. It is the only way in from the internet.
- The web tier. Two small Linux VMs run in different availability zones without public IPs, in a private subnet whose NSG admits HTTP and the load balancer's probes and nothing else. New virtual networks now default to private subnets with no hidden internet access, so the VMs go out through the load balancer's outbound rule. The servers keep no data, so any of them can be replaced from code in minutes.
- The data. Azure SQL Database accepts only Microsoft Entra identities, so no database password exists anywhere. In production it is zone-redundant, and its automatic backups allow point-in-time restore.
- The secrets. The application reads its settings from Key Vault through a managed identity, and Azure RBAC decides which identity may read which secret.
- The operations. Azure Monitor collects metrics and the activity log, a Log Analytics workspace keeps logs such as Key Vault's audit trail, and alert rules notify an action group that e-mails the on-call engineer.
- The guardrails. An Allowed-locations policy keeps resources in approved regions, tags feed cost reports, and a budget warns finance at 50, 80 and 100 percent.
- Everything as code. One Bicep deployment, split into modules, creates all of it. What-if previews every change, and a lost resource group is rebuilt in minutes rather than days.

Just as important is what this version leaves out on purpose. Shoppers still use plain HTTP; TLS and a web application firewall arrive with Application Gateway or Front Door in Lunch 27. The database still has a public endpoint, closed by its firewall; private endpoints replace it in the deep-dive month. Two VMs cannot grow by themselves for the 12.12 sale; scale sets with autoscale fix that in Lunch 23. Writing these gaps down is not an admission of failure. It is the honest backlog you hand to Ibu Sari together with the design, each item with its pillar and its price.

5. Answering the director: RTO and RPO

Ibu Sari's question has two halves. "How long can't we sell?" is the recovery time objective (RTO): the longest outage the business accepts. The half she has not asked yet — "how many orders could we lose?" — is the recovery point objective (RPO): how far back in time the last good copy of the data may be. Both are business decisions. Your job is to show what each design delivers and what it costs.

Go through the failures one by one; a single number for "the system" hides the detail that matters.

Failure | What the target design does | RTO | RPO
Today: the pantry server dies | Repair or buy hardware, reinstall, restore whatever backup exists | Days | Everything since the last backup, if there is one
One web VM crashes | The health probe marks it down; the other VM takes every new connection | Seconds (a few shoppers click again) | None — the web tier stores no data
A whole availability zone fails | Same for the web tier; a zone-redundant database keeps running in the other zones (Azure documents typically under 30 seconds) | Seconds to under a minute | None
Someone deletes today's orders | Point-in-time restore creates a copy of the database from just before the mistake | Minutes to hours, depending on database size | Minutes: transaction log backups run roughly every 5–10 minutes
The whole region is lost (rare) | Rebuild from Bicep in a second region; the data comes from a replica prepared there in advance (Lunch 28) | Hours without preparation; much less with a standby replica | Seconds with a replica; otherwise everything since the last copy outside the region

Numbers in a table are promises; only a drill turns them into facts. In the lab you switch off zone 1 yourself and time the gap, and Lunch 17's restore drill does the same for backups.

Warning: High availability is not a backup. Zone redundancy copies every change to the other zones within seconds — including the accidental DELETE. Only backups and point-in-time restore take you back to before the mistake. You need both, and you need to test the restore.

One more twist. Indonesia Central has no paired region, and features that rely on pairs are not available there — geo-redundant backup storage for Azure SQL, for example. A regional disaster plan must therefore name a second region explicitly (Southeast Asia is the natural choice), copy the data there on purpose, and allow that region in the Allowed-locations policy before the bad day.

So the answer for Ibu Sari becomes: "If a server, or even a whole datacenter zone, fails, we keep selling and lose nothing. If someone deletes orders, we restore to a minute before the mistake and re-enter a few minutes of orders. If the whole Jakarta region went down, today's design needs hours to rebuild elsewhere; a standby copy in Singapore would shrink that, and I can price it for you."

Pause and think: Ibu Sari asks for "zero downtime, zero data loss, and the cheapest option". Which two of the three can you offer at once, and which pillar does each combination spend?

6. What comes next: AZ-900 and the deep-dive month

If you plan to certify, the core month is your syllabus. Exam AZ-900 (Microsoft Azure Fundamentals) measures three skill areas — the skills measured as of July 20, 2026 — and every core lunch maps onto them:

Skill area | Weight | Lunches that teach it
Describe cloud concepts | 25–30% | 02 (plus the "why cloud" parts of 01 and 21)
Describe Azure architecture and services | 35–40% | 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15
Describe Azure management and governance | 30–35% | 01, 16, 18, 19, 20
Beyond the exam, but asked about at work | — | 17 (backup and disaster recovery); 21 pulls all three areas together

Three study tips. First, cloud concepts carry about a quarter of the marks but only one lunch, so reread Lunch 02 and its knowledge check twice. Second, open the official AZ-900 study guide (https://learn.microsoft.com/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-900) and tick off every bullet against this course; the exam uses current product names, so say Microsoft Entra ID, never Azure AD. Third, take the free practice assessment on Microsoft Learn, linked from the Azure Fundamentals certification page. It explains every answer, you can repeat it as often as you like, and its results show which lunches to revisit. A score of 700 or more passes the real exam.

Tip: The exam is also offered in Indonesian. Microsoft recommends registering with a personal Microsoft account, so your certification record stays with you when you change employers.

The core month gave you breadth. The deep-dive month takes each topic to the depth an administrator or architect needs, and it lines up neatly with Nusantara Retail's next requests:

Nusantara Retail's next request | Deep-dive lunch
"Rizky's pipeline must deploy without a stored password." | 22 · Identity and access (advanced)
"Survive the 12.12 sale without buying servers for the whole year." | 23 · Virtual machines (advanced)
"Make the invoices ransomware-proof and private." | 24 · Storage (advanced)
"Separate shared services from the workloads." | 25 · Virtual networking (advanced)
"Connect head office and forty stores." | 26 · Hybrid connectivity
"Block attacks and send shoppers to a healthy site." | 27 · Load balancing (advanced)
"Keep orders safe even if the region fails." | 28 · Relational databases (advanced)
"The microservices team wants Kubernetes." | 29 · Containers (advanced): AKS
"Why was checkout slow on Friday?" | 30 · Monitoring (advanced)
"Govern every subscription, not just one." | 31 · Governance at scale

The month ends with the advanced capstone challenge (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/32-advanced-capstone-challenge.html): requirements only, no step-by-step guide. You rebuild today's architecture the production way — hub and spoke, private endpoints, a web application firewall, a database failover group, and a disaster recovery plan for a region without a pair. Today's design is the one you can explain to Ibu Sari on Friday; that one is the one you would run.

Field notes from Stefanus

A number without a drill date is a guess. When someone shows me an RTO and RPO table, I ask one question per row: when did we last prove this, and who held the stopwatch? If the answer is "never", I write "untested" next to the number, in the same font size. My rule is that every failure scenario gets its own row, its own owner and its own next drill date — a zone failure can be rehearsed in an afternoon, a point-in-time restore in a lunch break. And I always hunt for the dependency nobody listed: a policy that blocks the recovery region, a secret only one person can read, a DNS record nobody owns. Recovery plans seldom break on the big steps; they break on the small permission nobody granted before the bad day.

Go further

- Azure Well-Architected Framework (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/) — the five pillars, service guides and design checklists, straight from Microsoft.
- What is an Azure landing zone? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ready/landing-zone/) — platform and workload landing zones with reference architectures; the starting point for Lunch 31.
- Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals (https://learn.microsoft.com/credentials/certifications/azure-fundamentals/) — exam details, the study guide and the free practice assessment.
- Azure Well-Architected Review (https://learn.microsoft.com/assessments/azure-architecture-review/) — a free self-assessment to run for the storefront after the lab.

quiz.q: Dewi suggests saving money by running only one web VM at night, when traffic is low. Which two pillars are in tension, and what is a reasonable compromise?
quiz.a: Reliability against cost optimization. Keep two small VMs in two zones around the clock (or a scale set with a minimum of two) and save elsewhere — burstable sizes, a reservation for the steady part, deleting test environments. Why: with one VM, a single failure at night is a full outage, and nobody is awake to fix it.

quiz.q: At 14:00 a faulty script deletes the day's orders. The database is zone-redundant. How do you get the orders back, and how much data do you lose?
quiz.a: Zone redundancy does not help — it replicated the delete within seconds. Use point-in-time restore to create a copy of the database as of just before 14:00, then copy the missing rows back or switch the application to the copy. You lose at most a few minutes of orders plus anything taken after the mistake; the restore time depends on the database size. Why: high availability protects against infrastructure failures; backups protect against data mistakes.

quiz.q: Before the storefront moves, Pak Budi wants the subscriptions, management groups, address ranges and baseline policies in place. Which Cloud Adoption Framework methodology is this, and what is its result called?
quiz.a: The Ready methodology; its result is an Azure landing zone — a platform landing zone plus workload landing zones. Why: Ready prepares the governed environment that workloads move into, before they move.

quiz.q: Your Allowed-locations policy permits only Indonesia Central. During a disaster recovery drill the team deploys the storefront to Southeast Asia. What happens, and what should have been done earlier?
quiz.a: The deployment is denied with RequestDisallowedByPolicy. The DR region should have been added to the allowed list (or covered by a separate assignment for the DR environment) as part of the DR plan, and tested in a drill. Why: guardrails must be designed together with the recovery plan, not discovered during the disaster.

quiz.q: A week before your AZ-900 exam, the practice assessment shows weak results on Azure Policy, resource locks and Microsoft Purview. Which skill area is that, how much does it weigh, and which lunches do you revisit first?
quiz.a: Describe Azure management and governance, 30–35% of the exam. Start with Lunch 18 (Azure Policy, locks, tags, Microsoft Purview), then 19, 16 and 20. Why: the practice assessment points to a skill area, and the course maps every skill area to lunches.

takeaways: The Well-Architected Framework's five pillars — reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence and performance efficiency — are questions to ask of every workload, and each design decision buys one pillar with another.

The Cloud Adoption Framework guides the whole organization through Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure and Manage; Ready produces an Azure landing zone (platform plus workload landing zones) before workloads move in.

Nusantara Retail's target architecture: a zone-redundant Standard front door, stateless VMs in two zones without public IPs, Entra-only Azure SQL, Key Vault with RBAC, Azure Monitor alerts, and policy and budget guardrails — all from Bicep.

Answer availability questions with an RTO and an RPO per failure scenario. High availability, backup and disaster recovery solve different problems, and Indonesia Central's missing pair means you choose and prepare the DR region yourself.

AZ-900 weighs cloud concepts at 25–30%, architecture and services at 35–40%, and management and governance at 30–35%; the free practice assessment shows where to revise, and the deep-dive month takes every topic further.

lab.title: Capstone project
lab.text:
What you'll build You deploy Nusantara Retail's core platform — the design the whole core month has been building — from one modular Bicep template: a private network, two web servers in two availability zones behind a Standard load balancer, an Azure SQL database that accepts only Microsoft Entra identities, a Key Vault that uses Azure RBAC, monitoring with three alert rules, an Allowed locations policy, and (in the portal) a budget. Then you treat it like production: you follow a request end to end, switch off zone 1 and prove the shop stays open, check every guardrail, answer the director's question with RTO and RPO, and review the design against the Well-Architected pillars. Bicep module | What it creates | Lunch infra/modules/network.bicep | vnet-nusa-capstone (10.21.0.0/16), private subnets snet-web and snet-data, NSGs nsg-web and nsg-data | 08 infra/modules/web.bicep | pip-nusa-shop, lb-nusa-shop, vm-web-1 (zone 1), vm-web-2 (zone 2) with their NICs and disks | 03, 06, 09 infra/modules/sql.bicep | logical server sql-nusa-, serverless database sqldb-orders | 11, 17 infra/modules/keyvault.bicep | kv-nusa-, secret sql-connection-string, your Key Vault Secrets Officer role | 15 infra/modules/monitoring.bicep | log-nusa, action group ag-nusa-oncall, alerts alert-web-cpu-high, alert-lb-backend-health, alert-web-vm-stopped, Key Vault audit logs | 16 infra/modules/policy.bicep | assignment allowed-locations of the built-in Allowed locations policy | 18 (portal, Task 7) | budget budget-lunch21 with 50/80/100% alerts | 19 infra/main.bicep | wires the six modules together; deploy.sh runs it with what-if first | 20 Before you start - An Azure subscription where you are Owner — Task 2 creates a role assignment and a policy assignment. Use a personal or dedicated lab subscription, never a company one (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). - Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. The Azure CLI and Bicep are already there. - A region with availability zones. The default, southeastasia, works; if you use indonesiacentral, run the environment check below first. You need 4 vCPUs of quota in the region (two Standard_B2ats_v2 web VMs with 2 vCPUs each). - An e-mail address you can read during the lab — the alerts go there. - Get the lab files and load the shared settings and this lab's names: git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git # first time only cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/21-core-capstone source ../common/config.sh source lab.env # resource names plus two helpers: who_answers and watch_shop echo "$RG" # rg-lunch21- bash ../common/check-environment.sh # optional: region, VM sizes and quota Important: The platform costs a little every hour it exists (two small VMs, a load balancer and a public IP; the database is free or pauses). Finish with Clean up, even if you stop halfway. Splitting the lab over several days? Run bash cleanup.sh at the end of each session and bash deploy.sh at the start of the next — rebuilding from code takes about 15 minutes, and that is exactly the point of infrastructure as code. Every time you open a new Cloud Shell session, go back to the lab folder and run source ../common/config.sh && source lab.env again before you continue. Session | Tasks | About 1 · Build | 1 Read the blueprint · 2 Deploy · 3 Follow a request | 50 min 2 · Prove | 4 Lose a zone · 5 Security and governance · 6 Operations | 65 min 3 · Decide | 7 Budget · 8 Answer the director · 9 Well-Architected review · Break it and fix it · Clean up | 65 min Choose your mode Mode | For you if… | How Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–9 below Challenge | you finished the core month and want to design it yourself | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way (your own Bicep is the best way), then run bash verify.sh Task 1 · Read the blueprint before you build In a real team nobody deploys a template they have not read. Reviewing infrastructure as code is how you catch an open port or a missing tag before it costs money. Open the files in the Cloud Shell editor (code infra/main.bicep) or read them on GitHub. ls -R infra Find each of these lines and say out loud why it is there: File | Look for | Why it matters main.bicep | network.outputs.webSubnetId | modules pass values to each other through outputs; Bicep orders the deployment from these references network.bicep | defaultOutboundAccess: false | a private subnet: VMs get no hidden internet access (Lunch 08) network.bicep | sourceAddressPrefix: 'AzureLoadBalancer' | the health probe must be allowed in, or every server looks dead web.bicep | zones: [ zone ] inside the VM loop | one VM per availability zone web.bicep | loadFileAsBase64('../../../common/cloud-init-web.yml') | the shared web server set-up, read at compile time; the path is relative to web.bicep web.bicep | disableOutboundSnat: true and outboundRules | explicit outbound access through the load balancer for the private VMs sql.bicep | azureADOnlyAuthentication: true | no SQL logins and no passwords; only Microsoft Entra identities sql.bicep | useFreeLimit and freeLimitExhaustionBehavior: 'AutoPause' | the free offer database pauses instead of billing you keyvault.bicep | enableRbacAuthorization: true and scope: vault | Azure RBAC for secrets, with your role on this vault only monitoring.bicep | three alert resources | capacity (CPU), application health (probe) and change (VM stopped) policy.bicep | e56962a6-4747-49cd-b67b-bf8b01975c4c | Bicep needs the built-in policy's ID; the comment shows how to check it Now let Bicep check the files: az bicep build --file infra/main.bicep --stdout > /dev/null && echo "main.bicep compiles" az bicep lint --file infra/main.bicep # no output means no linter warnings Checkpoint: main.bicep compiles is printed, and you can point to the module that creates each box in the diagram above. Quick test: which file would you change to add a third web server in zone 3? Answer web.bicep — add '3' to the zones parameter (and check your vCPU quota first). Task 2 · Preview and deploy deploy.sh does what a careful engineer does by hand: it finds out who you are (your user principal name and object ID become the Azure SQL administrator and the Key Vault secrets officer), makes sure you have an SSH key, compiles the templates, shows a what-if preview and only deploys after you say yes. bash deploy.sh Read the what-if output like a code review: every + Create line is something that will exist, cost money or change who can do what. You should see the network, the web tier, the database, the vault, its secret and role assignment, the workspace, the action group, three alert rules, a diagnostic setting and the policy assignment. A few lines may be marked as noise or ignored; that is normal. Type y to deploy. The deployment takes about 10–15 minutes, and the script then waits until the storefront answers. Tip: Prefer the portal? Watch the deployment while it runs: Resource groups › rg-lunch21- › Settings › Deployments. You see capstone plus one nested deployment per module (network, web, sql, keyvault, monitoring, policy), which shows the order Bicep worked out from the outputs. Note: Expect a few e-mails from Azure Monitor: one saying you were added to the action group, and possibly a backend health alert that fires and resolves while the web servers boot. That is your monitoring already working. Checkpoint: the deployment succeeded and the storefront answers. az deployment group show -g "$RG" -n "$DEPLOYMENT" --query properties.provisioningState -o tsv # Succeeded curl -s "http://$(lb_ip)/" | grep -o 'Served by.*

' | sed 's/<[^>]*>//g' Task 3 · Follow one request end to end A shopper's request crosses five things you built in the core month. Follow it hop by hop, so that later you can explain to anyone where it could break. 1. Who answers? Send ten requests. The load balancer hashes each new connection, so you see both servers and both zones. who_answers 10 2. The front door — a zone-redundant Standard public IP with a DNS name: az network public-ip show -g "$RG" -n "$PIP" \ --query "{ip:ipAddress, fqdn:dnsSettings.fqdn, sku:sku.name, zones:join(',', zones)}" -o table 3. The load balancer — health probe, rule and outbound rule: az network lb show -g "$RG" -n "$LB" \ --query "{probePath:probes[0].requestPath, everySeconds:probes[0].intervalInSeconds, rulePort:loadBalancingRules[0].frontendPort, outboundRules:length(outboundRules)}" -o table 4. The network security group — what may enter the subnet: az network nsg rule list -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" \ --query "[].{rule:name, priority:priority, from:sourceAddressPrefix, port:destinationPortRange, access:access}" -o table 5. The servers — private addresses only: az vm list -g "$RG" -d --query "[].{vm:name, zone:zones[0], privateIp:privateIps, publicIp:publicIps}" -o table 6. The way out. The VMs have no public IP and sit in a private subnet, yet they can reach the internet — through the load balancer's outbound rule. Ask a VM which address the internet sees (Run Command takes about a minute): az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --command-id RunShellScript \ --scripts "curl -s --max-time 10 https://api.ipify.org" --query "value[0].message" -o tsv lb_ip Tip: Prefer the portal? lb-nusa-shop › Monitoring › Insights draws the frontend, rule, probe and backend pool as a diagram with live health. rg-lunch21- › Resource visualizer shows how all the resources connect. Checkpoint: both vm-web-1 and vm-web-2 answer, the public IP lists zones 1,2,3, the VMs show no public IP, and the address the VM reports in step 6 is the same as lb_ip. Task 4 · Lose a zone, keep the shop open This is the moment the director cares about. You cannot switch off a real Azure datacenter, but you can remove everything you run in zone 1 — vm-web-1 — and watch what shoppers experience. 1. Deallocate vm-web-1 in the background and immediately start watching the shop for about two and a half minutes: az vm deallocate -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --no-wait watch_shop 150 You should see something like this: a mix at first, perhaps one or two (no answer) lines while the probe notices the server is gone, then only vm-web-2. 10:02:11 vm-web-1 10:02:13 vm-web-2 10:02:16 (no answer) 10:02:18 vm-web-2 10:02:20 vm-web-2 Count the (no answer) lines and multiply by two seconds: that is your measured RTO for a zone failure. Write it down; you need it in Task 8. 2. Confirm the VM is really gone and see who did it — the activity log records every control-plane action: az vm get-instance-view -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" \ --query "instanceView.statuses[?starts_with(code, 'PowerState/')].displayStatus | [0]" -o tsv az monitor activity-log list -g "$RG" --offset 1h \ --query "[?operationName.value=='Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action'].{time:eventTimestamp, who:caller, status:status.value}" -o table 3. Check your inbox. Within a few minutes the activity log alert alert-web-vm-stopped e-mails you: monitoring noticed the change before any customer complained. 4. Look at the probe's view: lb-nusa-shop › Monitoring › Metrics › Health Probe Status, aggregation Avg, then Apply splitting by Backend IP Address. The line for vm-web-1 stops — the load balancer does not probe a deallocated VM at all, which is why this lab also has the activity log alert. 5. Bring zone 1 back and watch it rejoin the rotation without any configuration change: az vm start -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" who_answers 10 Note: Variation — the application fails, not the server. Stop only the web service on vm-web-2. The VM keeps running, its health probe fails, the load balancer routes around it, and within about 5–10 minutes the metric alert alert-lb-backend-health e-mails you. Different failure, different signal. az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM2" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "systemctl stop nusa-web" -o none who_answers 6 # only vm-web-1 answers # ...wait for the e-mail, then repair it: az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM2" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "systemctl start nusa-web" -o none Checkpoint: the shop answered throughout (apart from a few seconds), you received the VM stopped e-mail, you wrote down your measured RTO, and who_answers 10 shows both servers again. Task 5 · Check the security and governance guardrails Security in this design is a stack of small, checkable decisions. Check them one by one. 1. Key Vault uses Azure RBAC, and you hold a role on this vault only: az keyvault show -n "$KV" \ --query "{rbac:properties.enableRbacAuthorization, softDeleteDays:properties.softDeleteRetentionInDays, purgeProtection:properties.enablePurgeProtection}" -o table KV_ID=$(az keyvault show -n "$KV" --query id -o tsv) az role assignment list --scope "$KV_ID" --query "[].{role:roleDefinitionName, who:principalName}" -o table 2. Read the secret. It is safe to print because it contains no password — that is the whole point of Microsoft Entra authentication. (A brand-new role assignment can take up to about 10 minutes to work; if you get Forbidden, wait and retry.) az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KV" -n "$SECRET" --query value -o tsv 3. Azure SQL accepts only Microsoft Entra identities, and nobody can connect from the internet yet: az sql server ad-only-auth get -g "$RG" -n "$SQL" --query azureAdOnlyAuthentication # true az sql server ad-admin list -g "$RG" -s "$SQL" --query "[].login" -o tsv # you az sql server firewall-rule list -g "$RG" -s "$SQL" -o table # empty az sql db show -g "$RG" -s "$SQL" -n "$DB" \ --query "{tier:currentServiceObjectiveName, autoPauseMinutes:autoPauseDelay, freeOffer:useFreeLimit}" -o table 4. The policy guardrail. List the assignment, then try to break the rule with a free resource (an empty NSG) in another region: az policy assignment list -g "$RG" --query "[].{name:name, displayName:displayName, mode:enforcementMode}" -o table OTHER_REGION=$([[ "$LOCATION" == "eastus" ]] && echo westeurope || echo eastus) az network nsg create -g "$RG" -n nsg-policy-test --location "$OTHER_REGION" Expected: an error with the code RequestDisallowedByPolicy and the message Nusantara Retail wrote into the assignment. A new assignment takes about five minutes to take effect; if the NSG was created, delete it (az network nsg delete -g "$RG" -n nsg-policy-test), wait a few minutes and try again. Tip: Prefer the portal? kv-nusa- › Access control (IAM) › Role assignments shows your role; sql-nusa- › Settings › Microsoft Entra ID shows the "Support only Microsoft Entra authentication" setting; Policy › Compliance shows the assignment (the first compliance results appear only after an evaluation cycle, which can take a while). Checkpoint: RBAC is true, the secret prints a connection string with Authentication=Active Directory Default and no password, Entra-only authentication is true, there are no firewall rules, and the out-of-region NSG was denied. Task 6 · Check the operations guardrails Operations answers three questions: will we know, will the right person hear about it, and can we find out what happened? 1. The alert rules and who they notify: az monitor metrics alert list -g "$RG" --query "[].{rule:name, severity:severity, enabled:enabled}" -o table az monitor activity-log alert list -g "$RG" --query "[].{rule:name, enabled:enabled}" -o table az monitor action-group show -g "$RG" -n "$AG" --query "{enabled:enabled, shortName:groupShortName, emails:length(emailReceivers)}" -o table In the portal, Monitor › Alerts (filtered to your resource group) lists the alerts that fired in Task 4. 2. Metrics without any agent. Azure collects host metrics for every VM: VM1_ID=$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM1" --query id -o tsv) az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM1_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" --interval PT5M --offset 1h --aggregation Average -o table 3. Logs: who read the secret? Your secret read in Task 5 was recorded. In the portal open log-nusa › Logs, switch to KQL mode and run this query (the first records can take 10–15 minutes to arrive): search "SecretGet" | where TimeGenerated > ago(4h) | project TimeGenerated, $table, OperationName | order by TimeGenerated desc search looks in every table, so it works whichever table your workspace uses for Key Vault logs (AzureDiagnostics by default). Lunch 30 teaches KQL properly. 4. Backups you did not have to configure. Azure SQL Database backs itself up; check the restore window: az sql db show -g "$RG" -s "$SQL" -n "$DB" --query "{earliestRestore:earliestRestoreDate, backupStorage:currentBackupStorageRedundancy}" -o table az sql db str-policy show -g "$RG" -s "$SQL" -n "$DB" --query retentionDays # 7 earliestRestore stays empty until the first full backup finishes, usually within about half an hour of creation. 5. (Optional) Make the CPU alert fire. Keep vm-web-2 busy for 15 minutes; within about 10 minutes alert-web-cpu-high e-mails you, and it resolves itself after the loop ends. az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM2" --command-id RunShellScript \ --scripts "nohup timeout 900 sh -c 'while :; do :; done' > /dev/null 2>&1 &" -o none Checkpoint: three enabled alert rules point to ag-nusa-oncall, you can see CPU metrics, your SecretGet appears in the workspace, and the database reports a 7-day restore window. Task 7 · Put a budget on it (portal, ≈10 min) Budgets are created in the portal here because that is where you set the e-mail alerts comfortably. A budget never stops resources; it warns people in time. 1. Portal › Resource groups › rg-lunch21- › Cost Management › Budgets › + Add. 2. Name budget-lunch21 (the scripts look for this name), Reset period Monthly, Amount a small number in your billing currency — for example the equivalent of US$10. 3. Next › Alert conditions: add Actual at 50, 80 and 100 percent, and Forecasted at 100 percent. Add your e-mail address under Alert recipients. 4. Create. Note: Cost data arrives with a delay of several hours, so a new budget shows little spending at first and alerts are never instant. If the Budgets page says your subscription offer is not supported, read the steps, skip the task, and expect verify.sh to show a note instead of a check. Checkpoint: az consumption budget list -g "$RG" --query "[].{name:name, amount:amount, period:timeGrain}" -o table Task 8 · Answer the director with RTO and RPO Ibu Sari asked: "If that server dies, how long can't we sell?" For each pillar, run the commands, mark every check , or , and finish the Trade-offs you accepted and Your top three improvements sections. Be strict: the lab build has several deliberate gaps (HTTP only, a database that is not zone-redundant, purge protection off) and the review is where you say so. Checkpoint: every check has a mark, at least three trade-offs are written down, and your top three improvements each name the lunch that teaches the fix. Break it and fix it Drift. Someone "tidies up" the network security group by hand and removes the rule for shoppers: az network nsg rule delete -g "$RG" --nsg-name "$NSG" -n Allow-HTTP-Internet curl -s -m 5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$(lb_ip)/" # 000 = no answer The shop is down — yet in the portal the load balancer's Health Probe Status stays at 100%. Why are both servers "healthy" while no shopper gets through? And what is the fastest safe way to repair it? Hint and fix The probe comes from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, which still has its own rule, so the servers look healthy. Shoppers come from the Internet tag, whose rule you deleted, and the default rules deny that traffic. Do not re-create the rule by hand — you might type a different priority or port. Run the template again: bash deploy.sh The what-if shows ~ Modify on nsg-web with the missing rule; confirm, and the shop is back. Infrastructure as code turns "what did someone change?" into a diff. To stop such changes in the first place, deploy the template as a deployment stack with deny settings (Lunch 20) — see the stretch goals. Verify your work bash verify.sh Every check should say PASS: network and NSG rules, both VMs running in zones 1 and 2 without public IPs, the zone-redundant Standard public IP and load balancer (probe, rule, outbound rule, two backends, HTTP 200 from both servers), Entra-only Azure SQL with TLS 1.2+ and a 7-day restore window, the RBAC Key Vault and its password-free secret, the workspace, action group, CPU and activity log alerts, Key Vault audit logs, the Allowed locations policy, and the budget. If a check fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. Clean up (do not skip!) bash cleanup.sh This deletes the budget, the policy assignment, your role assignment on the vault, the Key Vault itself (deleted and purged, so the name is free again), any deployment stack from the stretch goals, and resource group rg-lunch21- with everything in it. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes; check with az group list --tag lunch=21 -o table. Your SSH key in ~/.ssh stays — it is not an Azure resource.
